title: DataTrace: Benchmarking Data Agents for Evidence-Grounded Root-Cause Localization
comment: Accepted in KDD 2027 Datasets and Benchmarks Track
summary: Database agents diagnose pipeline failures, but a correct root cause is trustworthy only when it is supported by evidence the agent inspected. Existing benchmarks usually grade the final query or answer but fail to distinguish an evidence-based diagnosis from an unsupported correct answer. We introduce DataTrace, a benchmark for evidence-grounded root-cause localization over typed graphs of database artifacts. DataTrace uses controlled fault injection to derive root causes and evidence paths within 83 runnable environments without human annotations, and scores root-cause correctness and coverage of the supporting path separately. We also introduce CoSE, a generator-solver protocol in which an external verifier admits reproducible faults and checks both the submitted answer and the inspected evidence. Our evaluation shows that seven proprietary models achieve average root-cause accuracy 48%, with a mean per-model conditional unsupported rate of 18%. Fine-grained analysis shows that this gap varies sharply with fault mechanism, dependency distance, and evidence modality. After in-loop training on a matched held-out batch, the share of grounded correct diagnoses rises from 83.7% to 94.6%, while root-cause accuracy rises from 29.2% to 36.7%. These results show that while final-answer accuracy can hide unsupported diagnoses, evidence coverage provides an actionable signal to improve database agents. Code and data are available at https://hkustdial.github.io/datatrace/.

title: HorizANN: Elastically Scaling Vector Search with Ghost Edges
summary: Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) is fundamental to modern data-intensive AI applications such as retrieval-augmented generation, recommendation systems, and semantic search. Among existing indexing methods, graph-based indexes emerge as the state of the art due to their superior recall-throughput tradeoffs. Scaling these indexes to multiple machines requires partitioning the data and building indexes on each. However, when new machines are added or removed, the data must be repartitioned and the indexes reconstructed from scratch, making horizontal scaling costly at billion scale. In this work, we present HorizANN, a distributed graph-based ANNS system that scales horizontally without requiring full index reconstruction. To achieve this, we introduce ghost edges, a mechanism for preserving cross-partition connectivity as partition boundaries change during repartitioning. By reusing the structural information that would otherwise be discarded during repartitioning, HorizANN avoids costly full index reconstruction. As the index grows from 100M vectors on one worker to 1B vectors on ten workers, HorizANN inserts each 100M vectors within 2.5 hours and sustains 3.4--3.5K queries per second at 0.998 Recall@10.

title: HyperDBDiag: Multi-Root-Cause Identification and Operator-Level Localization for Database Performance Anomalies
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/Qiuzhidewang/HyperDBDiag
summary: Database performance anomalies in modern production environments are not always triggered by a single cause. Instead, they often arise from the concurrent interaction of multiple causes within the same time window, posing substantial challenges to accurate operator-level root-cause analysis. When multiple root causes interact through shared resources, metric anomalies may be amplified, attenuated, or masked. Consequently, salient local anomalies may no longer correspond directly to the actual root causes, making conventional single-path diagnosis and shallow correlation-based methods prone to misdiagnosis. To address this challenge, we propose HyperDBDiag, a method for multi-root-cause identification and operator-level localization of database performance anomalies. HyperDBDiag connects root causes, performance metrics, SQL templates, and execution operators in a knowledge graph, captures joint anomaly patterns across metrics with a metric hypergraph, and uses a constrained LLM to determine the final root-cause set and provide remediation suggestions. When finer-grained localization is possible, HyperDBDiag also identifies the associated anomalous SQL statements and execution operators. We evaluate HyperDBDiag on a database performance anomaly dataset constructed using DB-MAGS. Experimental results show that HyperDBDiag effectively reduces graph complexity while improving root-cause localization accuracy.

title: KaleidoKV: Rearranging Evidence for Efficient KV Cache Reuse in Offline RAG Inference
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) augments large language models (LLMs) on question-answering (QA) tasks with retrieved evidence at inference time. Related questions in an offline batch often retrieve overlapping evidence, but prefix caching reuses key-value (KV) states only for identical token prefixes, making reuse dependent on evidence order. Although all questions and evidence are known before execution, existing reordering methods commit to early grouping decisions and can miss sharing opportunities that require several requests to move together. Evaluating alternative layouts can incur planning costs that offset inference savings, while concurrent requests may still recompute shared prefixes before their KV states become available. To address these challenges, we propose KaleidoKV, a framework that plans evidence orders across the batch and controls when requests enter the engine while preserving each request's evidence set and content. Joint layout planning revises formed groups through coordinated request moves and keeps a move only if it lowers planned prefill, the computation required when each shared prefix is computed once. A global prefix index selects evidence orders by locating reusable prefixes and evaluates each move incrementally from only the affected request paths. Prefix-ready admission tracks nested prefix dependencies, delaying requests whose shared prefixes are still being computed while allowing independent requests to proceed. Experiments on four QA workloads and four LLMs show that KaleidoKV achieves the highest throughput and lowest mean time to first token in all 16 settings, with approximately 1.24-1.75x the throughput of the strongest baseline, including planning time. With Llama-3.1-8B under the default configuration, actual prefill stays within 0.5% of planned prefill across all four workloads.

title: More Secure Software Development via Cultural Analysis: How could Log4Shell happen?
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures. Written as a magazine article for IEEE Privacy and Security, hence the overly short abstract
summary: There is little progress avoiding vulnerabilities. Cultural analysis may help: For a given team, find the specific cultural values that led to a past vulnerability, then modify the values accordingly for the future. After enough such studies, patterns will likely emerge that are useful for the development community at large.

title: Coordinating Distributed AI Servers with Industrial Loads to Reduce Grid-Interconnection Needs
comment: Submitted to IEEE PES General Meeting 2027. Code and data: https://github.com/ruikelyu/distributed_LLM
summary: We show that co-locating distributed AI servers with industrial demand and coordinating AI workloads with production loads can substantially reduce the additional grid interconnection that AI computing requires. Grid interconnection is increasingly constraining the expansion of large AI data centers. Factories already have grid connections sized for their peak production loads, and we propose hosting AI servers during production valleys. We formulate a joint optimization that sizes CPU and GPU servers, schedules deadline-constrained tasks, and routes tasks among factories, and use it to compare three factory-site architectures with new large data centers serving the same demand. Applying this framework to 31 Chinese manufacturing industries, we find that AI demand and production loads often do not peak together. As a result, AI servers placed at factories and scheduled according to production peaks need about 60% less additional interconnection capacity than new large data centers, and 98% less when tasks are routed among a group's factories.

title: Read Boundaries in Agent Memory: Consistency, Completeness, and Repair
summary: Agent-memory services assemble evidence through several reads across connections or stores. An update between those reads can pair an assertion with source content from another revision. We protect the complete recall, including enrichment and materialization, and evaluate the resulting evidence and service behavior in Hindsight and Cognee. A 600-run Cognee study compares unprotected recall, a repeated recall, a read/write lock, and optimistic epoch validation under default incremental updates and full rebuilds. At approximately 20 recalls/s, unprotected default updates yield 199 conflicting responses among 12,010 scheduled recalls with spaced writes and 284 among 12,010 with bursts. The lock and epoch validation each deliver complete, compatible evidence for all 24,020 default-update recalls. With default bursts, epoch validation reduces update p95 by 109 ms while adding 290 ms to recall p95 relative to the lock. A separate 160-run incremental-failure study distinguishes mixed revisions from complete new derived content whose canonical source record remains old. Both protected policies refuse service after failure; the first default retry restores all 80 fault runs through native full-rebuild fallback. In Hindsight, a shared PostgreSQL snapshot removes the mismatch in ten controlled pairs, with recall p95 rising from 19 ms to 29 ms. These results identify the read boundary needed for coherent evidence and the publication and recovery conditions governing service after an update fails.

title: Mining Architectural Models in the Wild: A Curated Dataset of AADL Models
comment: Accepted for publication in the ICSME 2026, Tool Demonstration and Data Showcase Track (The 42nd IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution). 5 pages
summary: Empirical research on software architecture maintenance and evolution is hindered by the scarcity of large-scale, validated, and richly annotated model datasets. Existing benchmarks are limited in scale, provide only model-level annotations, or lack alignment with reference architectures, thereby restricting reproducible studies of architectural reuse, conformance, and AI-driven analysis. To address this gap, we present A3D, a curated dataset of 1,115 Architecture Analysis and Design Language (AADL) models mined from public GitHub repositories and validated with the OSATE tool. The dataset spans 7 generic domains and 52 specific-problem clusters, and provides two annotation layers: (i) domain- and problem-level labels, which capture different model aggregation criteria, and (ii) component-level mappings to three reference architectures, which have been externally validated through a user study. Models are released in AADL and JSON formats with full provenance, a reproducible mining pipeline, and the validation protocol.

title: Supercharging Olmo-core for Efficient and Scalable MoE Training
comment: 169 pages. Web version and video: https://www.taotianhua.com/olmo-core-moe/
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models add parameters without proportionally increasing per-token compute. However, training cost also depends on bytes moved, memory held, and kernels launched, and many of those costs follow total parameter size rather than active compute. On infrastructure built for dense models, this mismatch is costly: in early baselines, throughput fell as stored expert parameter size grew, even though the useful work per token stayed nearly fixed. To close this gap, we present a redesigned training stack in Olmo-core, built for efficient, scalable MoE training. We replace the Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) of earlier Olmo-core versions with an architecture built on Distributed Data Parallel (DDP), and add Expert Parallelism (EP), Pipeline Parallelism (PP), a distributed optimizer, and activation recompute. We propose NVSHMEM-based rowwise EP, which writes each token directly into its expert's buffer, avoiding dispatch and combine permutation overhead. We make EP fully synchronization-free by keeping routing metadata on the GPU and using device-scheduled grouped GEMMs. Closely integrated MXFP8 cuts compute, activation-memory, and transport costs, and topology-agnostic checkpoints let the parallel layout change between runs. On NVL8 B300 nodes, the stack supports training configurations from 12.9 billion to 1.2 trillion total parameters on up to 512 GPUs, reaching 858 useful-model TFLOP/s/GPU at 1.2 trillion with MXFP8 and per-layer recompute; an experimental capacity test with the optional DeepEP v2 backend reaches 2.38 trillion. We also explain each design choice and share findings for other training systems; for example, we identify a failure pattern we call Token Gerrymandering, in which the MoE router can learn to hack the load-balancing loss, and find that overlapping communication with computation can slow the overlapped kernels by more than it hides.

title: CapCover Filter: Semantic Approximate Membership Queries over Embeddings
summary:
Determining whether an embedding is sufficiently similar to any vector in a vector store without performing a nearest-neighbor search can substantially improve query throughput in vector-store systems. We study Semantic Approximate Membership Queries (SAMQs), which allow queries to be rejected when no indexed vector meets the requested similarity threshold, while guaranteeing no false negatives.
  We introduce CapCover Filter, a geometric data structure that summarizes a set of embeddings using spherical caps. Its representation is independent of the query threshold, allowing a single filter to support arbitrary thresholds without reconstruction. We evaluate alternative construction and quantization methods, compare CapCover Filter with competing filters, and measure its impact on query throughput.
  Across five real-world datasets, at a cosine similarity threshold of 0.95, CapCover Filter eliminates approximately 20--100\% of index accesses while using only 2\% of the raw (FP32) embedding memory. When placed before a FAISS flat index, it improves query throughput by up to 382\% and by approximately 116\% on average across the five datasets, while returning the same range-search result. We also evaluate lower similarity thresholds. Our results show that CapCover Filter can substantially improve vector-store throughput when similarity thresholds are tight, retrieval is expensive, and indexed embeddings are highly clustered. We release an optimized implementation of CapCover Filter and its evaluation framework.

title: Software Engineering Practice in the Virtual Reality/Augmented Reality Software Life Cycle: A Systematic Survey
comment: Preprint. Manuscript submitted to IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering. 27 pages
summary:
Leveraging diverse virtual reality (VR) technologies, VR provides users with an immersive experience in a computer-generated 3D virtual environment. In contrast, augmented reality (AR) superimposes virtual objects (such as images, text, animations, etc.) onto users' real scenes. Both VR and AR have received increasing attention due to the maturity of computer graphics, computer vision, and artificial intelligence. VR and AR have gained rapid market growth in both hardware and software. In the early stages, VR/AR-related research mainly focused on hardware (e.g., head-mounted displays and sensor-equipped controllers). Recently, VR/AR software has become a hot topic due to the mature VR/AR ecosystem. However, there is no comprehensive work to summarize software engineering practices in VR/AR.
  To bridge this gap, this paper aims to provide a systematic survey summarizing the state-of-the-art research on VR/AR from the perspective of software engineering practices. Considering the general VR/AR software life cycle, we categorize the relevant research based on the VR/AR software life cycle, including requirement engineering and planning, software design, software development, software testing, software deployment, software maintenance and updates, and software evaluation and feedback. As for each stage above, we summarize relevant research on VR/AR for this stage, including the design of technical routes, the construction of datasets, and the design of evaluation metrics. We also enumerate existing empirical studies and make comparisons with conventional software (e.g., mobile/desktop application development). In summary, our article can help researchers gain a comprehensive understanding of the achievements of the existing software development techniques in the VR/AR field and also provide insights, which may facilitate the benign development of VR/AR software ecosystem in the future.

title: NVFP4-MLA: Unified FP4 KV-Cache Storage and Attention Computation for Multi-Head Latent Attention
summary: Long-context reasoning and agentic workloads make key-value (KV) cache capacity and attention computation the dominant costs of serving frontier large language models. We present NVFP4-MLA, the first design to push both KV-cache storage and attention computation of multi-head latent attention (MLA) to FP4. NVFP4-MLA co-designs the quantization algorithm with the attention kernel and the cache system. Selective residual compensation preserves model accuracy by adding NVFP4 residuals only to the quantization-sensitive channels. Two-dimensional quantization blocks make the shared latent cache compatible with the different reduction directions of the two attention batched matrix multiplications (BMMs), removing requantization between them. On DeepSeek-R1 and Kimi-K3, NVFP4-MLA matches BF16 MLA average accuracy across nine benchmarks while compressing the MLA KV cache by 3.20x and 3.05x relative to BF16 MLA. On NVIDIA Rubin GPUs, NVFP4-MLA speeds up the attention kernel over FP8 MLA by up to 2.82x on DeepSeek-R1 and 2.71x on Kimi-K3, and lowers p90 time to first token in agentic multi-turn serving by up to 3.5x and 2.1x, respectively. In disaggregated DeepSeek-R1 serving, it also raises per-GPU throughput by up to 2.30x.

title: Optimizing Query Decomposition for Reliable Validation
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) have made querying databases more accessible, but cannot guarantee that the SQL they generate is correct. Without a trusted reference query, a validator (human or LLM) must decide whether a generated query answers the intended question. Enterprise questions often require queries with multiple joins, nested subqueries, and multi-level aggregation, and validating such a query in one judgment is error-prone. Decomposition simplifies this task by rewriting a query into smaller queries (blocks) that recompose to the original, each checked against its own sub-question.
  Decompositions differ, however: smaller blocks make each judgment easier but require more judgments, and the best balance depends on the validator's ability. We formulate validation-aware query decomposition as an optimization problem. Just as a query optimizer chooses among equivalent plans by estimated cost, we choose among decompositions by how reliably a given validator is expected to check them. We model how task difficulty and validator ability jointly affect reliability and define an objective that balances reliability against the number of judgments. Over a space of decompositions derived from logical-plan rewrites, our search finds an optimal one. We implement it in DecoVal, a pipeline that presents each block with its sub-question and input interface, combines local verdicts into a query-level decision, and localizes errors to blocks.
  A user study shows that decomposition helps human validators catch and locate errors: with DecoVal, participants caught 91% of the errors, up from 36% without decomposition, and located the error in nearly every rejection. Experiments on BEAVER and Spider 2.0 with LLM validators show that DecoVal also raises error-detection recall over whole-query validation while keeping precision high, and that the best granularity depends on the validator.

title: Use of Peer Code Review to Identify Potential Security Vulnerabilities in Open Source Software: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: Context: Security vulnerabilities in OSS can have severe consequences. OSS project participants widely use peer code review to improve quality and prevent security flaws. However, despite mandatory reviews, OSS projects still contain vulnerabilities, highlighting the need to evaluate code review effectiveness for security. Objectives: This SLR synthesizes evidence on vulnerability types identified or missed, security practices, tool support, reviewer challenges, and factors that improve detection. Method: Searches of five digital libraries yielded 1,067 studies, of which 20 were included. Vulnerabilities were categorized using the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) framework. Results: Peer code reviews effectively detect localized, well-known vulnerabilities (e.g., buffer overruns, race conditions, crashes, XSS) but often miss subtle, complex, context-dependent issues (e.g., input validation weaknesses, access control weaknesses, resource lifecycle weaknesses). Effective security practices are associated with reviewer expertise, code familiarity, frequent small changes, and organizational support. Security analysis tools, especially Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools, reduce reviewer effort and improve detection but cannot replace human judgment. Reviewers continue to face limitations in security knowledge, experience, time, and understanding of complex systems. Effectiveness improves through security training, domain expertise, contextual familiarity, formalized review processes, and supportive review environments. Conclusion: Peer code review contributes to OSS security but is insufficient on its own. Improving effectiveness requires structured review processes and checklists, security training, organizational incentives, and lightweight automated tool support to help reviewers detect subtle vulnerabilities while reinforcing secure development practices.

title: Can Agentic LLMs Write Task-Based Parallel Code? A Study of OpenMP Tasking, HPX, StarPU and TTG
summary: Task-based programming offers more expressive power than loop-level parallelism, but the runtimes providing it differ widely in API style, maturity, and the amount of public code to learn from. This paper asks how well LLM agents write C++ for four of them: OpenMP Tasking, HPX, StarPU, and TTG. Instead of single one-shot prompts, we use an agentic workflow in which the model edits files, compiles, and runs its kernels until it reproduces a reference output. Five locally hosted open-weight LLM implement seven HPC kernels, including matrix multiplication, Cholesky and LU factorization, in all four frameworks and a serial baseline to verify their understanding of the problem in general. Every kernel is evaluated independently for correctness at each concurrency level, strong scaling, and peak memory. Model capability dominates the outcome: three models produce correct, genuinely task-parallel kernels in 57-82% of the cases, while two models rarely compile their own code and almost never succeed. For the capable models, OpenMP Tasking and HPX are handled most reliably, StarPU is close behind, and TTG trails. The best generated GEMM and factorization kernels match or exceed the multithreaded OpenBLAS/LAPACK reference. However, correctness overstates parallel quality: several "parallel" kernels contain no parallelism at all; and serialized task graphs and unsuitable task granularity remain common.

title: A Gaussian Primitive Data Management Framework for Efficient 3DGS Trajectory Rendering
summary: Trajectory rendering, which renders novel views of a reconstructed 3D scene along a camera path, is a core operation in digital twins and autonomous inspection. Structured 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renders a single view in real time by decoding sparse anchors into Gaussians on demand, but it renders a trajectory view by view: every view projects all anchors to select them, re-decodes anchors already requested by neighboring views, and runs all steps on the GPU while the CPU idles. We treat this as a spatial data management problem, where anchors are spatial objects, views are range queries, and decoded Gaussians are shared derived data, and propose GDM-GS, which removes redundancy at three levels. Within a view, an anchor index and an occluder index answer each view as a holed-frustum range query, so out-of-view and provably hidden anchors are never decoded. Across views, shared materialization decodes each requested anchor once per group of consecutive views while preserving each view's selection. Across processors, a hybrid pipeline balances selections between the CPU and the GPU before grouped decoding under bounded memory. Experiments on large-scale public scenes show that GDM-GS substantially reduces trajectory rendering latency while preserving image quality.

title: Knowledge-Centric Automated Issue Resolution: A Systematic Survey and Taxonomy
summary: Automated issue resolution is a knowledge-intensive software maintenance task in which LLM-based agents must acquire, represent, use, and update knowledge from repositories, execution environments, historical artifacts, documents, tools, and prior repair processes. This paper presents a systematic survey of 133 studies on automated issue resolution from a knowledge-centric perspective. We introduce a three-layer taxonomy that organizes issue-resolution knowledge into the Background Knowledge Layer, the Repository Knowledge Layer, and the Procedural Knowledge Layer, and analyze the knowledge lifecycle along six dimensions: knowledge types, sources and extraction methods, representation formats, usage methods, workflow stages, and temporal evolution. Our analysis shows that current systems primarily rely on Existing Code Knowledge and Development Tool Knowledge, while Repository Evolution Knowledge and Experiential Knowledge are increasingly adopted, indicating a shift toward history-informed, feedback-aware, and experience-oriented issue resolution. In contrast, Design Architecture Knowledge and explicitly modeled Background Knowledge remain comparatively underexplored. These findings suggest that future systems should move beyond temporary context construction toward reusable, traceable, and evolvable software knowledge infrastructures that support more controllable, verifiable, and generalizable software engineering agents. The surveyed studies and related resources are maintained at https://github.com/SYSUSELab/Awesome-Knowledge-for-AIR.

title: IA-MoE: An Intensity-Aware Mixture of Experts for DNN Inference
comment: 8 pages, 9 figures. Accepted manuscript of a paper published at IEEE ICNSC 2025
summary: With the ever-increasing parameter scale and structural complexity of deep neural network (DNN) models, traditional cloud-based inference encounters bottlenecks in performance, privacy protection, and energy efficiency. While edge computing and edge intelligence facilitate the migration of inference tasks to edge servers closer to the data source, existing end-edge-cloud collaborative inference still encounters critical challenges, such as sensitivity to heterogeneous resources, complexity in multi-objective optimization, and adaptability to dynamic workloads. To achieve the joint optimization of end-to-end latency and energy consumption under dynamic inference requests with multi-resource constraints, we propose IA-MoE, an intensity-aware Mixture of Experts (MoE) framework. By modeling the model partitioning problem as a bilateral matching problem between layer tasks and virtual machine resources for each inference request, IA-MoE dynamically partitions DNN models in an edge-cloud hybrid computing environment. We evaluate IA-MoE using three representative DNNs (i.e., AlexNet, VGG16, ResNet50) on two public inference datasets in an enhanced CloudSimSDN simulation environment. Experimental results demonstrate that IA-MoE outperforms baseline methods regarding weighted normalized metrics for end-to-end latency and energy consumption. To our knowledge, this is the first study to introduce the MoE paradigm for DNN partitioning and collaborative inference in hybrid computing environments, providing a practical solution for efficient inference in artificial intelligence applications.

title: QuarkDB: A Hybrid Database System for Quantum Data Management
summary: Emerging quantum applications like quantum communication generate large volumes of high-dimensional quantum data, requiring efficient data analysis and storage. However, classical database systems often struggle to meet requirements such as quantum processing or version management. This paper presents QuarkDB designed for efficient quantum data management. QuarkDB establishes a unified object model for relational and quantum data and defines the syntax of Quantum Structured Query Language. To support efficient quantum data management, QuarkDB integrates three key components: (1) a Hybrid Query Engine with cost-based hybrid plan selection over classical and quantum operators, (2) an Execution Engine with a three-level instructions intermediate representation, QuarkDB-IR, to support quantum execution and reduce quantum processing costs, and (3) a Storage Engine supporting quantum data version management, state reconstruction and data reuse. Compared with classical databases such as SQLite and PostgreSQL or quantum databases like Qute, our QuarkDB achieves query-latency speedups ranging from 2.14x to 25.86x speedup under extensive real-world workloads.

title: Towards Sustainable Large Language Model Inference: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: Large language model (LLM) inference is becoming a significant contributor to both operational cost and environmental impact in modern AI deployments. Energy consumption during inference depends on multiple factors across the pipeline, including input and output length, model design, system-level decisions, and hardware characteristics. This paper presents a systematic literature review (SLR) of energy-efficient and sustainable LLM inference. We analyze selected primary studies to identify techniques proposed to reduce energy consumption across different levels of the inference pipeline, including input, model, system, and hardware. We further examine the trade-offs between energy consumption, latency, and accuracy, highlighting inconsistencies in how these relationships are evaluated. In addition, we review the tools, datasets, and metrics used for energy measurement, covering both software-based and hardware-based approaches. This survey provides a comprehensive synthesis of existing literature, offering insights into the effectiveness of different techniques in terms of energy savings and their associated impact on accuracy. It highlights the trade-offs between energy efficiency and performance and identifies limitations in current evaluation practices. Overall, this work aims to support future research toward more efficient and environmentally responsible deployment of LLMs. Our repository of relevant references is maintained on GitHub.

title: Two-Robot Evacuation from a Unit Disk in the Segment Visibility Model
summary: Under segment visibility, two robots discover a target as soon as it belongs to the segment joining their positions, even if neither robot has physically reached it. We study two unit-speed robots starting at the center of a unit disk that must both reach an exit (target) placed at an unknown point of its boundary. In our model robots are permitted to leave the disk while searching. We give a three-phase tangent-and-arc algorithm whose exact worst-case evacuation time is 2\sqrt{3}+π/3 \approx 4.511299$. We also prove a matching lower bound for the class of descending horizontal full-slice sweeps, allowing asymmetric robot trajectories. The proof uses an exterior path-length inequality and a feasible minimum-half-width symmetrization. Determining the optimal time over all segment-visibility algorithms remains open.

title: Tight Width Minimisation of Self-Join-Free Quantified Conjunctive Queries
summary: Query minimisation is a classical problem in database theory and the width of a formula, defined as the maximum number of free variables over all subformulae, is a central measure for query evaluation. We study width minimisation for a subclass of quantified conjunctive queries (QCQs), namely self-join-free QCQs. For this subclass, we show that rewriting optimality coincides with semantic optimality: given a query $φ$, the minimum-width query obtainable from $φ$ by applying natural and established rewriting rules has minimum width among all first-order formulae logically equivalent to $φ$. As a consequence, the width of a self-join-free QCQ can be optimised by a logical-equivalence-preserving rewriting algorithm.

title: Loop Engineering: Version-Bound, Evidence-Gated Coordination for Production Coding Agents
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Sanitized supporting data included in the source package. Zenodo preprint DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21504929
summary:
Coding agents can edit repositories and execute tests, yet production software work extends far beyond code generation. It requires durable task context, scoped authority, version-aware approval, source-independent verification, interruption recovery, and accountable handoffs between humans and automated workers. We present Loop Engineering, a method for operating multiple asynchronous agent loops over shared, auditable repository state without relying on private conversational handoffs. Each loop is specified by six elements: a trigger, a context projection, an authority boundary, a verifier, a stop condition, and a write-back rule. Versioned procedural contracts, called Skills, encode reusable operating policy; a Harness bounds the available action surface and collects evidence; human gates authorize high-consequence transitions against exact artifact versions.
  We report a design-and-experience study from MewDesign, a revenue-generating commercial AI design product. Five specialized loops cover planning, scoped implementation, review, test release, and reconciliation. A cross-sectional audit contains 50 durable marker records across 26 GitHub work items. Five pull requests reached a version-bound test lock: three proceeded to test releases with runtime evidence from sources distinct from the deployment request, and two stopped before merge. A detailed drift episode shows one observed fail-closed path: a new commit invalidated prior approval and evidence, and the workflow refused to reuse stale continuous-integration results. The study is not a controlled benchmark and does not establish causal productivity or general safety. It provides early evidence of feasibility, traceability, and bounded progression in one production setting.

title: Making Preemption Productive in Long-Output LLM Serving
summary: Reasoning LLMs generate long outputs whose key--value (KV) caches occupy GPU memory for minutes. When memory fills, the server preempts requests, and a preempted request can repeatedly lose and recover its state while producing little new output. We call this behavior KV thrashing. In certain cases, existing systems leave more than a fifth of requests stalled for over a minute. Because preemption cannot be avoided without delaying admission, we ask how to make it productive. We present Stint, a serving system that preserves a preempted request's work, bounds how long it waits, and gives it fresh output after it returns. Stint stores fixed-length KV snapshots in a contiguity-first CPU pool with an exact-extent allocator, and moves them with fused K/V gather/scatter kernels and double buffering. Age-based readmission brings stalled requests back, and protection gives them a turn of fresh decoding before another preemption. Remaining-length estimates from decoding hidden states guide victim selection. On olympiad-math replays with Qwen3-32B on H200 GPUs, no request pauses for more than 50 seconds under Stint and p99 time per output token falls by 50.7\% relative to recomputation in the same engine. The replay as a whole finishes 10.7\% sooner (12.0\% higher throughput), because the requests that baselines starve no longer finish last.

title: Adaptive-Elbow Graph Traversal for Schema Retrieval in Text-to-SQL
comment: Presented at the 5th Italian Conference on Big Data and Data Science (ITADATA 2026). To appear in CEUR Workshop Proceedings
summary: LLM-based natural-language interfaces to relational databases are gated by a schema-retrieval step: the generator can only be as good as the slice of schema it is shown. On a database with hundreds of tables, that slice must be selected and the selection is two-sided---omit a needed table and the query becomes unrecoverable, include too many and the irrelevant ones act as noise that degrades the model's output. When an agentic retriever that lets the model inspect the schema can be too costly or too slow, the fallback is an embedder that ranks tables by cosine similarity and keeps a top-k. This fallback has two weaknesses: a fixed budget is suboptimal question by question, and embedding similarity overlooks foreign-key-linked tables that are necessary for joins. We present Adaptive-Elbow Graph Traversal (AEGT, ElbowHop for short), a property-graph table retriever that addresses both: an adaptive elbow cutoff replaces the fixed budget with a per-question one under a single aggressiveness parameter, and bidirectional foreign-key traversal deterministically recovers the bridge tables embedding similarity misses. We evaluate the retriever on 3 corpora of increasing candidate-pool size (BIRD Mini-Dev queried per database, 3--13 tables; its eleven schemas merged, 74; and a merged Spider-train graph, 546) and isolate the two mechanisms under a per-question budget-matched protocol. Across these settings the adaptive elbow emerges as the dominant mechanism---at matched recall it roughly doubles precision over a fixed budget on the larger pools, the margin widening as the pool grows---while the foreign-key traversal pays off on the join-critical bridge tables dense retrieval cannot reach, in the single-hop tight-budget case. We characterize the method as a low-cost, recall-robust first stage for schema retrieval on which a downstream selection or generation step can build.

title: Where AI Use Is Normalized, Author Seniority but Not AI Disclosure Biases Code Review
summary: Code-review tools increasingly display whether an author used AI when preparing pull requests. Recent studies report that AI disclosure makes reviewers rate otherwise identical work as less competent, with the penalty falling hardest on already-marginalized authors. In a within-subjects experiment in an AI-normalized organization, 447 software engineers each reviewed the same four code snippets under an AI-use disclosure embedded in the commit message and author-seniority labels. AI disclosure did not bias perceptions of code effectiveness or author competence, whereas a seniority label significantly biased both. Together, these findings show no detected penalty for disclosed AI use in this setting, while confirming that the author information shown in code review can still bias evaluations.

title: TileCache: Serving Multi-Round Diffusion Image Editing with Compressed Activation Caches
summary: Multi-round diffusion image editing can reduce computation by reusing intermediate activations, but retaining these activations across editing rounds introduces substantial memory and bandwidth overheads. Compression can reduce these overheads, but efficient cache construction is challenging: compressing only after editing requires buffering over 100 GB of activations per request. Moreover, the compressed cache must support selective reuse, as future masked edits require only a subset of the cached activations. It also exposes a scheduling challenge, as cached edits are faster than initial generations, causing naive policies to severely delay either initial generations or editing requests. In this paper, we aim to address both challenges through compression-informed serving. We develop TileCache, a serving system for multi-round diffusion editing. It compresses reusable activations and incorporates a scheduler that balances both edits and initial generation requests. Compared with the state-of-the-art image editing baseline, TileCache sustains over 2x the request arrival rate at 90% SLO attainment. It completes edits 2.4-4.5x and initial generations 1.3-2.2x faster than the baseline, while preserving image quality.

title: LoopSkill: Evidence-Bound Lifecycle Control and the Safety-Liveness Tradeoff in Coding Agents
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures. Exploratory and nonconfirmatory study; artifact efficacy is reported separately from workflow closure
summary: Coding agents can edit repositories and announce completion, but conversational claims do not prove that artifacts, dispatches, state versions, and authority still agree. LoopSkill is an evidence-bound lifecycle control plane with a schema-validated sole writer, durable outbox routing, artifact-bound reports, recovery, independent review, and heartbeat-gated finalization. We evaluate a locally frozen v3.3.12 integration under a common 1,800-second budget on a selected subset of SWE-bench Lite. The original 140-cell plan was administratively truncated after interim outcomes were visible, so the 60-cell analysis is exploratory and nonconfirmatory. Of 58 scored cells, blind artifact success was 7/19 for LoopSkill, 11/19 for implementation plus independent review, and 14/20 for an ordinary coding agent; two cells were apparatus null. Across 18 complete LoopSkill-versus-review pairs, the descriptive risk difference was -0.222 with exact McNemar p=0.125. No scored LoopSkill workflow finalized. The results expose a safety-liveness and fixed-budget cost tradeoff. They do not establish comparative superiority, long-horizon efficacy, or a false-accept rate.

title: Benchmarking LLM Inference on Desktop-Scale NVIDIA Grace Blackwell Clusters
comment: 24 pages, 16 figures, 8 tables. Code and data available at https://github.com/kevinhbhimani/dgx-spark-llm-serving-benchmark Copy
summary: Two NVIDIA DGX Spark GB10 systems connect directly over 200 GbE to serve larger language models and increase inference capacity, but the benefits depend on how they are deployed. We benchmark 17 open-weight checkpoints spanning dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, 8B to 235B parameters and four weight precisions on one and two RDMA-connected systems. Using vLLM, we compare tensor parallelism (TP=2), pipeline parallelism (PP=2) and a two-replica baseline at concurrency 1 to 64, with three independent launches per configuration. TP=2 delivers a median 1.59x peak-throughput gain over one Spark, versus 1.39x for PP=2 and has higher throughput in 93 of 96 matched comparisons with separated 95% Welch intervals. It reduces unloaded inter-token latency to 0.52x to 0.73x of one Spark, whereas PP=2 provides little reduction. TP=2 also achieves the highest goodput under a strict 100 ms inter-token latency objective wherever both strategies are supported and the objective is met. For models fitting on one Spark, TP=2 generally favors low-concurrency serving, while replication offers higher throughput at high concurrency. One Spark uses less GPU energy per output token at matched concurrency. Across three precision ladders, NVFP4 reduces unloaded latency more than adding a second Spark at BF16. NCCL microbenchmarks and comparisons with an earlier TCP campaign suggest that collective communication overhead contributes to the advantage of TP=2. These results provide deployment guidance for desktop-scale inference.

title: Predictive Test Optimization Without Historical Failure Data
comment: Accepted for the Industry Track of the 42nd International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution
summary: As software systems grow in size and complexity, their test suites become increasingly expensive to execute, delaying feedback and wasting resources. State-of-the-art predictive test optimization methods use machine learning to select tests relevant to a change, typically trained on historical failures. This depends on failure histories and is susceptible to label noise from flaky tests. We introduce the novel method of co-evolution labeling for predictive test optimization, deriving test relevance from tests and code changing together in the version history. These data are widely available and less noisy. We train and evaluate models with failure and co-evolution labels on three large projects---from industry and open source; each with thousands of tests and more than 1M LOC. Co-evolution labeling nearly matches the failure detection capabilities of failure-based models, with an overall Average Percentage of Faults Detected of 0.88, while being more resistant to label noise and requiring no test result history. Co-evolution labeling offers a practical, immediately deployable path to faster pipelines and reliable predictive test optimization.

title: Beyond Service Discovery: Coverage Awareness in LLM-Driven Service Composition
summary: Large language models increasingly support the automated discovery and composition of services. In federated data ecosystems, this creates new opportunities for reusing existing data products and transformation services when constructing service-based data exchange modeled as data-sharing pipelines. However, finding relevant reusable assets does not imply that the available assets are sufficient to satisfy a consumer request. In this paper, we distinguish reuse discovery, the ability to identify relevant published assets, from reuse coverage, the extent to which the available assets support the transformations required by a request. We further consider coverage awareness, the ability of a composition system to recognize insufficient coverage. We investigate this distinction using PipeFinder, an LLM-driven framework for composing data-sharing pipelines, and evaluate 99 consumer requests against a fixed catalogue of data products and transformation services. Our experiments show that relevant data products can be discovered reliably, while successful composition remains considerably more difficult. More importantly, when required transformation services are missing, the framework typically constructs a pipeline from the available services rather than recognizing that the request cannot be satisfied. Explicitly incorporating coverage checking into the planning procedure substantially improves recognition of such cases. These results suggest that coverage awareness should be treated as an explicit concern in LLM-driven service composition and cannot be assumed to follow from improved discovery or model capability.

title: A Survey of Image-to-Code Generation for Software Engineering
summary: A large fraction of software intent is expressed visually before it is implemented. A designer hands a screenshot or a Figma mockup to a front-end engineer, an architect sketches a UML diagram or a flowchart, and a bug report ships with a picture of what went wrong. Turning such visual artifacts directly into executable software has therefore become an active problem at the intersection of computer vision and software engineering. The present survey organizes the literature on image-to-code generation for software engineering, defined as the family of methods whose input contains a visual modality and whose output is software an engineer would otherwise write by hand. We deliberately scope the survey to software-engineering code, namely user-interface and front-end code, code recovered from software diagrams such as UML and flowcharts, program repair and test code driven by visual signals, and general software-code targets, and we exclude adjacent code-generation domains whose home communities lie elsewhere, such as chart plotting scripts, vector-graphics programs, hardware description languages, and robot policies. Rather than cataloguing systems in isolation, we introduce a unified processing pipeline of visual understanding, component recognition, layout reasoning, code planning, code generation, and verification, and organize the survey around its stages. We trace five overlapping eras from rule-based reverse engineering to agentic generation, survey each pipeline stage and each software-engineering task in depth grounded in what individual systems actually do, consolidate the datasets, benchmarks, and metrics, and lay out the open challenges of design-system generalization, long-horizon and interactive generation, cross-framework deployment, accessibility, hallucinated components, and unreliable evaluation.

title: Top-Level Operational Equilibrium: When is the response of a distributed system predictable from its own telemetry?
comment: 38 pages, 1 figure, 14 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/vikcas/TLOE-theoretical_analysis (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24200155)
summary: Distributed systems deployed across the edge-cloud continuum are adapted continuously: scaled, re-routed, given more or less capacity. Each adaptation rests on an expectation of how the system will respond, yet operators cannot tell from the telemetry they already collect whether that response is predictable. We define top-level operational equilibrium (TLOE), a notion of equilibrium for a running system, stated relative to the controls its operator declares. TLOE has three conditions: stationarity with time-scale separation, sufficiency of a top-level aggregate for the controls, and time-reversibility of that aggregate. We prove that an aggregate satisfying the last two exists if and only if the minimal sufficient statistic of the controls is time-reversible, so the coarsest admissible aggregate is derived rather than chosen. Under the first two conditions, the response to a small control change follows from passive telemetry through the steady-state fluctuation-response identity, with a conjugate observable fixed by the type of control: the total work in progress for a change of load, the occupancy of a stage for a change of its capacity. For chains of exponential single-server stages with Poisson input, TLOE holds exactly for load control at every stable throughput, but never for a control on the capacity of the first or last stage. On reference models, a per-stage conjugate overestimates the early response about threefold, blocking between stages breaks both conditions weakly, and a hysteretic autoscaler leaves no admissible aggregate at any reaction time computed. We specify a test for each condition, show that a static sufficiency test with an estimated top-level conjugate has no power, and quantify on simulated telemetry the window lengths the prediction and the reversibility test need. The evidence is on reference models; real telemetry is left to future work.

title: Measuring and Optimizing Energy Efficiency in ICT: A Multi-vocal Literature Review on Data Centers, Cloud Computing, and LLM-Driven Code Optimization
summary: Rapid growth in Information and Communication Technology (ICT) increases electricity use and environmental impact. Addressing this challenge requires a systematic, software-centric view of how energy and related sustainability attributes are measured, reported, and improved. We present a comprehensive Multi-vocal Literature Review (MLR) integrating peer-reviewed and gray literature to map current practice in measuring and optimizing energy use in ICT software, with emphasis on data centers and cloud computing environments (DCCCEs). First, we synthesize how sustainability is measured across ICT by proposing a taxonomy organized along metric domains (power/energy, energy efficiency, environmental impact) and component granularity (from applications, to containers/VMs, and system-of-systems levels). We summarize measurement approaches and the tooling landscape that implements them. Second, we review optimization strategies at the software and system levels, covering dynamic power and resource management, VM/container consolidation, energy-aware software and system design, and cross-layer, system-wide methods relevant to DCCCEs. Third, we examine how large language models (LLMs) are applied to code generation and transformation for resource-efficient software, noting that most studies target code generation (predominantly in Python) and evaluate runtime and memory, with fewer works directly reporting energy. Hardware- and network-level telemetry are treated as data sources for software-level analysis. We identify gaps in vendor-neutral telemetry, consistent measurement and reporting practices, network-level metrics, and unified, cross-layer optimization frameworks, and outline directions for improving reproducibility and comparability. We screened 635 records (2010-2025) and included 181 sources (122 peer-reviewed, 59 gray).

title: Investigating the Impact of CI-Source Sensitivity in Carbon-Aware Resource Management Systems
summary: The sustainable growth of data centres increasingly depends on Resource-Management Systems (RMSs) that aim to reduce carbon emissions of computing workloads without degrading performance. This need is intensified by the rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) workloads, which demand exponentially growing amounts of compute and energy across geographically distributed infrastructure. Recent carbon-aware RMSs exploit temporal and spatial variation in grid Carbon Intensity (CI) to shift workloads towards lower-carbon periods or locations. In practice, CI estimates and forecasts can be inaccurate and uncertain, and CI providers' methods differ substantially. Such discrepancies may have a significant impact on RMS placement decision-making, raising concerns about the fragility of existing solutions. Thus, in this work, we ask how discrepancies between plausible CI estimates propagate into resource-management decisions and operational outcomes. To answer this question, we harmonise and characterise CI traces from Wattnet and ElectricityMaps across five Central European zones. We then propose our evaluation framework: External CI Signal Characterisation And Perturbation Evaluation (ESCAPE), which assesses provider switching and controlled CI perturbations in a reproduced placement setting. We implement our framework using CarbonEdge as a use case, and measure changes in placement decisions and operational outcomes, such as carbon proxy, energy use, and latency. Our results show that switching CI-source changes the dominant placement site in 43.50% cases, and alters reported operational outcomes. These changes occur despite high rank correlation and structured disagreement between CI-sources. This observed sensitivity to CI-source choice motivates robustness-aware carbon-aware placement, in which CI uncertainty should be explicitly accounted for in resource-allocation decisions.

title: Formal Modeling in Software Engineering with LLMs: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: Formal verification provides strong correctness guarantees for software systems but remains hindered by the substantial expertise and manual effort required to construct and maintain formal models. The recent rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) has prompted growing interest in whether their natural language understanding and generation capabilities can be leveraged to automate labor-intensive modeling activities. This paper presents a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) examining how LLMs have been applied to automate model checking and the generation of formal and semi-formal models within software engineering. The review follows established SLR methodologies and a PICOC-driven search strategy across four major digital libraries. From an initial search of 1,193 articles, 34 peer-reviewed conference, journal, and workshop articles published between 2022 and April 2026 were selected and analyzed using a structured data extraction form. The review identifies six recurring trends in the literature, including the automated generation of formal models for model checking, LLM-assisted downstream formal verification, iterative and repair-based generation pipelines, and the generation of semi-formal UML and SysML artifacts whose underlying techniques are transferable to formal modeling contexts. Across these trends, LLMs are generally found to perform well on syntactic generation and repair tasks but struggle with semantic correctness, motivating widespread use of counterexample-guided repair loops, intermediate representations, and human-in-the-loop validation. Notably, this review finds that the use of LLMs specifically to automate model checking remains a largely unexplored area, with comparatively little research published on this narrower task.

title: A Matter of Stages: Energy-Latency Trade-offs in Multimodal LLM Serving
summary: Online serving of multimodal large language models requires deciding whether to separate visual encoding (E), prefill (P), and decode (D) across GPUs and how to configure their frequencies. EPD disaggregation enables independent stage control, but it also changes communication and queueing behavior. Lowering one stage's frequency can increase queueing and prolong execution across the EPD pipeline. Consequently, reducing power at one stage does not necessarily reduce total GPU energy per request. In this paper, we systematically characterize fused and EPD-disaggregated serving across four multimodal models under a fixed three-GPU budget, followed by single-stage and uniform downclocking experiments across 18 workload combinations. We find that disaggregation reduces GPU energy per successful request by 13.3-37.0% at nearly identical output-token throughput, but increases mean TTFT. Downclocking exhibits distinct stage sensitivities, and aggressive frequency reductions can offset power savings through queueing and longer execution. Across the evaluated workloads, uniform downclocking to 80% reduces GPU energy by 11.7-18.6% with modest mean-latency changes. Guided by these findings, we develop a budgeted frequency exploration strategy to select energy-efficient configurations under latency constraints. Evaluation shows that four probes can identify the lowest-energy feasible configuration among 25 measured candidates across all 288 evaluated positive-margin SLO scenarios. These results provide practical guidance for energy-efficient multimodal serving.

title: Uncertainty in Cyber-Physical Systems: A Literature Survey
summary: Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) operate in dynamic, dependable environments where sensing, communication, decision-making, control, and assurance are affected by uncertainty. This paper characterizes CPS uncertainty through a literature survey comprising 186 primary studies. We (i) characterize uncertainty types, (ii) identify uncertainty sources, (iii) relate uncertainty to life-cycle phases in which they occur, and (iv) overview the possible uncertain mitigation strategies. The findings show that uncertainty is most often conceptualized as an assurance issue. Safety and specification uncertainty is the most prevalent category, followed by environmental and model/epistemic uncertainty. Domain mapping reveals broad cross-domain engagement, while safety-critical sectors such as autonomous systems, energy systems, and robotics CPSs display domain-specific uncertainty patterns. The life-cycle analysis indicates that uncertainty is not limited to the development or testing phases but also arises during runtime operation, underscoring the need for continuous assurance approaches. Mitigation strategies primarily include runtime monitoring, robust and adaptive control, and probabilistic reasoning. In summary, this survey contributes to a thorough characterization of CPS uncertainty and provides a discussion of articles on this topic.

title: GNoF: A Low-SM-Overhead GPU-Native NVMe-over-Fabrics Completion Path for Data-Intensive GPU Workloads
summary:
GPUs are the main compute engine for data-intensive workloads whose datasets exceed device memory and reside on remote flash. The conventional host CPU orchestrates every NVMe-over-Fabrics (NVMe-oF) transaction and stages data through host memory, costing high CPU usage, repeated CPU-GPU synchronization, and redundant data movement. GPU-initiated storage removes the CPU from the I/O path, but existing designs leave two problems: synchronous lock-step completion pins streaming multiprocessors (SMs) in spin-polling, wasteful over a 10-100 microsecond RDMA round trip, and current GPU-native remote systems focus on target-side firmware while using per-command doorbells and periodic CQ polling.
  We present GNoF, a GPU-native NVMe-oF/RDMA data path where GPU threads build command capsules, post send work-queue elements, ring doorbells, and reap completions entirely on the device; the CPU only handles one-time connection setup, the admin queue, and a keep-alive thread. Three mechanisms target long fabric round trips: a doorbell mover that coalesces a burst's doorbells into one MMIO ring; a batched CQ poller with a lock-free fast peek and monotonic completion counters that cannot lose a wakeup; and a set-associative, reference-pinned GPU page cache with split fetch/wait pipelining and orphan-fill takeover. GNoF needs no target or firmware change and runs against an unmodified SPDK target.
  On a 200 Gb/s InfiniBand fabric, GNoF reaches 1.77 million 4 KB IOPS per client at 0.37% host CPU and about 1% SM occupancy, versus 40% CPU for kernel nvme-rdma and about 100% SM occupancy for lock-step polling. Against three existing baselines (kernel nvme-rdma, BaM over a BlueField-3 DPU, and BaM on a local SSD) under identical workloads, we show 10-22x gains on selective column I/O, CPU-burn immunity, and the regime where bulk staging is faster.

title: Model-Driven Approaches for DevOps: A Systematic Literature Review
summary:
DevOps integrates tools and methodologies aimed at optimizing software development, building, deployment, and monitoring by automating and reducing the development lifecycle and improving software quality. However, despite its many advantages, it presents notable challenges, particularly in terms of usability and migration. On the other hand, model-driven engineering (MDE) offers a way to abstract from specific technologies and implementation details, which can be leveraged to improve these aspects, as happens in software development.
  In this paper, we present the first systematic literature review aiming to understand the current MDE approaches for supporting DevOps development. We focus on categorizing the works based on computing domains, the phases of the DevOps process to which they contribute, and the reengineering steps they propose.
  Our findings highlight a dominant focus on cloud computing, while some studies propose domain-agnostic approaches. We also observe that the deployment and integration phases are the most explored. This reveals research opportunities regarding both the domains and DevOps phases addressed.
  We also found limited use of text-to-model transformations, while nearly half of the papers employed model-to-model transformations. Text-to-model transformations were more prevalent overall. Most notably, we discovered that no study proposed a complete reengineering process, which represents an exciting avenue for future research.

title: The Bipartible Architecture Pattern: Transparently Directing HTTP Requests over InfiniBand
comment: Presented at 8th International Workshop on Containers and New Orchestration Paradigms for Isolated Environments in HPC
summary:
Large-scale compute (HPC) systems with coherent-memory workloads often deploy InfiniBand (IB) networks for high-bandwidth and low-latency inter-node and storage communication. A separate TCP network is typically used for control-plane and general-purpose communication. The last decade has seen the rise of cloud-native software patterns. These patterns are characterized by container-based software distribution and inter-node and storage communication over TCP/IP. In an unoptimized HPC environment, a cloud-native workload will typically use HTTP for some or all communication.
  This paper introduces the Bipartible architecture pattern to optimize cloud-native workload traffic in HPC environments. This paper focuses on optimizing HTTP storage service requests. These requests are transparently transformed onto IB traffic without modifying workload implementation or network configuration. This is achieved by 'cloning' a global HTTP service (BPService) onto the HPC cluster compute host(s) where the workload executes at scale. Provided the global persistent storage is on the IB network the HTTP service requests are returned to the workload via IB and not TCP/IP.
  The feasibility of this pattern is demonstrated by implementing a prototype BPService for S3 and a Hybrid-BPService (service metadata is accessed over TCP, bulk data over IB) for a software repository service. We offer this pattern in addition to many alternative approaches to address the performance challenges of executing workloads written to cloud-native design patterns in HPC environments. Finally, while the initial results are encuraging signficant validation of any service must be performed under both read and write scenarios before deployment into production is planned.

title: Automatic techniques for security bug report identification: A systematic mapping study
summary:
Several studies have investigated the use of automated techniques to help practitioners identify security bug reports early in the defect management process. However, currently there is no comprehensive overview of this research area. Such an overview will help identify future research directions and consolidate the potentially relevant existing solutions. This study aims to provide a comprehensive overview of automated techniques for identifying security bug reports. To achieve this, we conducted a systematic mapping study and identified 28 primary studies.
  The study's findings show that the literature has evaluated various automatic techniques for identifying security bug reports, including traditional machine learning, deep learning, and more advanced large language models. The two main challenges identified are the lack of labeled data and data imbalance. Furthermore, we observe that existing studies lack evaluations in real industrial settings and rely mostly on archival data from open-source repositories. The most commonly used data sources in these studies include Wicket, Ambari, Camel, and Derby. Overall, the literature appears fragmented, highlighting the need for future work to focus on comprehensive evaluations of the most promising techniques.

title: Lower Bounds for the Distributed Computation of Degeneracy and k-Core
summary: The degeneracy of a graph $G$ is the maximum integer $k$ such that $G$ has a non-empty $k$-core, where the $k$-core is the largest induced subgraph with minimum degree $k$. Computing the $k$-core of a graph $G$ is P-complete. In the decentralized setting, the sequential peeling algorithm can be distributed so that the core value of every node, i.e., the largest integer $k$ for which the node belongs to the $k$-core, is computed in $O(n)$ rounds in $n$-node networks, where adjacent nodes exchange only $O(\log n)$ bits at each round, i.e., in the standard CONGEST model. However, while $Ω(D)$ rounds is a trivial lower bound for these problems in networks of diameter $D$, this does not rule out the existence of an algorithm running in $O(D)+o(n)$ rounds in CONGEST, as it is the case for many very important graph problems, including MST. We show that it is unlikely that such an algorithm exists, or, if it does exist, then it requires $\tildeΩ(\sqrt{n})$ rounds. Specifically, our first main result states that, for any $ε>0$, approximating the degeneracy up to a multiplicative factor $2-ε$ requires $\tildeΩ(\sqrt{n})$ rounds in CONGEST even in networks of diameter $O(\log n)$, and still $\tildeΩ(n^{1/3})$ rounds in networks of constant diameter. We also show that improving this lower bound seems challenging, as we demonstrate that the newer frameworks cannot be used as black boxes to obtain a better lower bound for degeneracy. Our second main result provides a better bound, albeit conditional. It states that, unless the well-known circuit value problem (CVP) admits a parallel polynomial speedup -- an outcome considered unlikely -- it holds that, for every $ε>δ>0$, deciding whether a graph is 2-degenerate cannot be solved in $O(D+ n^{1-ε})$ rounds with $O(n^δ)$-time parallel local computation per round at each node.

title: AI Cannot Review What Humans Catch: A First Look at the Reviews of Agent Instruction Files
summary: Agents increasingly shape software, and instruction files steer them. Files such as AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, and SKILL.md act as executable policy: prose that a machine reads and acts on. Unlike ordinary documentation, a single edit to one of these files can silently redirect how an agent behaves across an entire repository. Natural-language rules have no per-change oracle, so they slip past the compilers, type-checkers, and test suites that guard code. Review is therefore the only quality gate, but no prior work has studied how that review happens. We analyzed 2,870 instruction-file pull requests across 2,246 repositories. The gate is largely broken: over 70% of instruction-file changes receive no substantive review. When an AI reviewer substitutes for a human, it is structurally blind to the concerns that most need human judgment. It catches surface structure but misses factual errors, necessity questions, and staleness problems. We contribute the first taxonomy of instruction-file review concerns (16 categories), which exposes this sharp human/AI divergence, and a benchmark of 1,962 human-checked concerns across 468 PRs. We ran three widely-used agents (Codex, OpenCode, and Claude Code) against the benchmark, giving each reviewer the full repository at review time. They recovered only 1.3-3.9% of the concerns humans raise. Even the strongest current agents cannot substitute for human attention on these files.

title: LLMs in DevSecOps: A Systematic Mapping of Models, Evidence, and Research Gaps Across the Software Lifecycle
comment: 15 Pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. This manuscript has been accepted for publication at the 2026 proceedings of the World Congress on Computer Science, Computer Engineering, and Applied Computing (CSCE 2026)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into software security and DevSecOps workflows, yet their adoption, evaluation, and maturity vary substantially across lifecycle stages. This study systematically maps recent LLM-enabled security research published between 2024 and 2026 (until June) across six DevSecOps stages: \textit{Plan}, \textit{Code}, \textit{Test}, \textit{Review}, \textit{Deploy}, and \textit{Monitor}. For each stage, we analyze the security tasks addressed, models and adaptation strategies employed, evaluation settings, reported effectiveness, and key limitations. Our findings reveal an uneven research landscape, with \textit{Test} and \textit{Code} receiving substantially greater attention than \textit{Deploy} and \textit{Review}. Across stages, recent systems increasingly rely on structured context, iterative reasoning, fine-tuning, retrieval augmentation, or agentic workflows rather than direct single-shot prompting. However, reported performance remains difficult to compare because studies use heterogeneous tasks, datasets, metrics, and baselines. Furthermore, most approaches are evaluated using benchmarks or open-source repositories, while industrial-scale evidence remains limited. We also find that existing systems are predominantly stage-specific, with little evidence of LLM-enabled security reasoning spanning multiple DevSecOps stages. Based on these observations, we identify research opportunities in standardized evaluation, production-scale validation, supply-chain and Infrastructure-as-Code security, trustworthy autonomous remediation, and cross-stage LLM integration. This study provides a recent lifecycle-level view of where LLM-enabled DevSecOps research is concentrated, what methodological patterns are emerging, and where significant gaps remain.

title: Benchmark Factory: Agentic Benchmark Creation via Dataset Curation and Label-Free Quality Anchors
comment: 5 pages, prepared for submission to AGENT 2027
summary: Teams deploying coding agents need benchmarks built from their own code, but curating and validating them by hand is resource intensive, and an unvalidated benchmark can mislead silently. We present Benchmark Factory, an autonomous meta-agent loop with human checkpoints: an LLM agent writes sourcing queries over landed production code changes, runs models of known relative strength on each candidate, diagnoses why a candidate fails, and repairs it by editing its queries, prompts, and configuration until it clears quality anchors that need no per-task human labels. We used Benchmark Factory to build benchmarks for five developer cohorts at our organization. Engineering raters scored a 5% sample 2.3 for task quality and 2.6 for grader verdicts on a 1-to-3 scale. On configurations never used to build them, the benchmarks ranked Claude Opus~4.7 at high reasoning effort above low effort (60.6% vs. 54.4% of tasks passed, $p=0.002$) and GPT-5.5 above GPT-5.4 (65.8% vs. 60.5%, $p=0.004$); 9 of the 10 per-cohort comparisons pointed the same way. A deliberately trivial benchmark failed the anchors; five broken graders failed them, even under a relaxed rule fixed in advance that the real grader passes; and with model labels shuffled so that no true ordering existed, random redraws of a candidate passed in at most 1.4% of simulations. The anchors are necessary, not sufficient, conditions for a valid benchmark, designed to focus human review on what the loop cannot repair.

title: Revisiting Re-executability: Coverage-Guided Symbolic Feedback to Improve Decompilation
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures. Yuxin Hu and Xiaohan Wang contributed equally
summary: When source code is unavailable, decompilation provides a source-level representation of a binary. However, code recovered by conventional or LLM-assisted decompilation may not preserve the original behavior of the binary. Recent approaches evaluate re-executability using fixed test suites, but passing these suites does not ensure behavioral preservation. We present SymDec, an LLM-assisted decompiled-code repair system that uses the original binary as a behavioral reference. SymDec uses coverage-guided symbolic execution to explore the I/O-level behavior of the original and recompiled binaries, and symbolic comparison to identify inputs that expose behavioral differences. These inputs are replayed on both binaries to confirm the differences, which are returned as structured feedback to guide subsequent LLM revisions. We evaluate SymDec on 120 functions from ExeBench and DecompileBench, compiled for x86-64 and ARM64 at optimization levels O0-O3, yielding 960 binary decompilation tasks. More than half of the tasks yield candidates that pass the supplied test suite and complete symbolic comparison without detected behavioral differences. Among candidates that pass all supplied tests, symbolic comparison exposes replay-confirmed behavioral differences in 4.5% of cases, showing that test-suite re-executability can miss behavioral discrepancies. Under the same input-generation budget, symbolic execution achieves higher mean line and branch coverage than black-box fuzzing. Symbolic feedback also improves the conventional metric, increasing the mean single-step test-pass rate from 90.1% to 93.3%. These results show that symbolic comparison provides stronger evidence of behavioral consistency than test-suite re-executability alone and supplies effective feedback for repairing decompiled code.

title: Level Up! AI-Driven Challenges and Adaptations to Code Review Practices
summary: AI can write code faster than humans can review, causing a bottleneck and necessitating changes to code review practices. This bottleneck is hotly debated, giving rise to two extreme and orthogonal imagined futures: one where humans continue to be firmly entrenched in the review process, and one where AI agents merge pull requests entirely without human involvement. Yet, these futures remain rooted in folk wisdom. Through a mixed-methods study of interviews ($n = 24$) and a survey ($n = 2{,}590$) at a large, multinational software company with widespread access to AI, we identify AI-driven code review challenges and strategies reported as effective to meet them. We found that AI enables, necessitates, and complicates a shift in the human reviewer's role toward high-level concerns (e.g., design and intent). We found that AI-assisted authoring results in increased burden for reviewers due to challenges such as a lack of author stewardship and PR volume and size, potentially leading to downstream debt. Our survey showed AI review usage was not correlated with less difficulty keeping up with PR volume, indicating using AI for review alone is not sufficient for solving AI-driven review challenges. Developers found the most useful strategies to be organizations supporting and resourcing review, pushing review burden upstream, and prioritizing reviewer attention on the concerns that matter most.

title: Mining Unity VR Repositories for Refactoring Patterns and Technical Debt
summary:
Maintaining virtual reality (VR) applications poses challenges tied to real-time performance, hardware dependencies, and complex interactions. Yet little is known about how developers refactor these applications, which kinds of technical debt they address, or how well automated tools capture VR-specific changes. We mined 1,755 candidate refactoring commits from 176 open-source Unity VR repositories and manually examined a sample of 303 commits, of which 270 contained at least one refactoring. We also extended RefactoringMiner to create VRRefMiner, a tool that detects conventional refactorings in C# scripts used by Unity applications.
  Our analysis found both conventional and VR-specific refactorings. VR-specific changes addressed concerns such as interaction logic, performance, and Unity-specific artifacts. Code debt was the most prevalent category overall, while interaction debt and UI/UX debt were the main categories addressed by VR-specific refactorings. Across the repositories, VRRefMiner detected 15,549 operations spanning 68 refactoring types, with structural moves and extractions accounting for 31.0% of detections. It detected conventional refactorings in 216 of 246 commits labeled as general refactoring. In the 24 commits labeled as VR-specific, the tool could detect conventional changes but identified no VR-specific refactoring categories. These results point to a need for detection techniques that account for both source code and the Unity artifacts involved in VR maintenance.
